catalog_quote: In Papuan Malay, primary stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable of the lexical root, while secondary stress is assigned to the alternating syllable preceding the one carrying the primary stress. These stress patterns apply to lexical roots (§2.4.4.1) as well as to lexical items that are historically derived by (unproductive) affixation (§2.4.4.2). ... Most disyllabic roots have penultimate stress (900/1,004 items – 90%), as illustrated in Table 2.39. The remaining 104 items (10%) have ultimate stress and display the following pattern. In 101 of the 104 roots (97%), the unstressed penultimate syllable contains the front open-near vowel /ɛ/. ... Front open-near /ɛ/, however, does not condition ultimate stress, as in 61 of the 900 lexical roots with penultimate stress (7%) the stressed syllable also contains front /ɛ/. ... The data presented in Table 2.39 to Table 2.41 demonstr…
sweep_summary: Papuan Malay is in the catalog as fixed-unreviewed (penultimate primary stress of the root, secondary on alternating preceding syllables; ~10% roots with ultimate stress, 97% of them with /ɛ/ in the penult), deciding source Kluge 2017 (open-access reference grammar, sect. 2.4.4, pp. 96-99). The 8 stress/prosody-titled items are all Kaland/Himmelmann-circle work from 2018-2020. Read in full: Kaland, Himmelmann & Kluge 2019 ICPhS (downloaded; first-hand random-forest analysis of Kluge's corpus: penult 932 / ult 108; ultimate stress only when the penult has /ε/ and the final syllable has no mid vowel — refines the exception statement), Riesberg et al. 2020 Lab. Phonology (downloaded by automated download default UA past the Anubis bot-check; restates Kluge's 90/10 distribution, calls the acoustic support 'some, though not particularly strong', and concludes PM listeners barely agree on prominences — a caution on the status of 'lexical stress', not on position), plus the already-held Kaland 2018 SP (spectral tilt confirms Kluge), Riesberg et al. 2018 (same caution, p. 407) and Kaland, Bracks & Himmelmann 2018 (silent). Abstract-only: Kaland & Baumann 2020 JASA and Kaland & Himmelmann 2020 Lang. & Speech (both phrase-level/discourse prosody, silent on placement). Still unread: Kaland 2019 J. Phonetics (the flagship acoustic confirmation; hybrid-OA but ScienceDirect/Elsevier API could not be reached by automated download, and the author-hosted copies on sfb1252.uni-koeln.de listed in Kaland's CV are unreachable because every uni-koeln.de host refuses connections by automated download; the Internet Archive was offline) and Kaland, Kluge & van Heuven 2021 Phonetica (same host). Net: coding confirmed and refined; no source supersedes Kluge 2017; suggested edits are an evidence-grade upgrade citing Kaland et al. 2019 ICPhS / Kaland 2018 / Kaland 2019 as instrumental confirmation, the sharper exception rule, and a caution line for the Riesberg et al. 'stressless Malayic' position.

new_statements.quote: Word stress in Papuan Malay occurs mostly on the penultimate syllable, except when this syllable contains /ε/ [11]. For example, in /tε.ˈkan/ ('to press') stress moves to /kan/ because /ε/ could reduce to schwa, which cannot be stressed. Thus, in /ˈtu.kan/ ('craftsman') stress occurs on the default penultimate syllable. [...] ultimate stress is mainly found when /ε/ occurred in the first syllable, confirming [11]. [...] When the penult contains /ε/, stress shifts to the ultimate syllable only when the ultimate does not contain a mid-vowel.
new_statements.citation: Kaland, Constantijn, Nikolaus P. Himmelmann & Angela Kluge. 2019. Stress predictors in a Papuan Malay random forest. Proceedings of the 19th ICPhS (Melbourne), 2871-2875.

new_statements.reading: First-hand corpus analysis (with the grammar's author) of the same 1,040-root word list underlying Kluge 2017: primary stress is penultimate by default (932/1,040, 90%); the 108 ultimate-stress roots are those with /ε/ in the penult whose final syllable lacks a mid vowel, leaving 33 residual exceptions (<4%). This is a fixed-penultimate system with a lexically restricted, vowel-conditioned shift to the final syllable — the same coding the catalog holds, with a sharper statement of the exception condition. Complemented by Kaland 2018 (spectral tilt) and, as reported in Kaland 2021 pp. 9-10 and Riesberg et al. 2020 p. 3, Kaland 2019 (duration, vowel quality, tilt), which acoustically confirm Kluge's stressed/unstressed distinction; Riesberg et al. 2018/2020 add the caution that native listeners do not perceive this as a prominence distinction.

new_statements.quote: [p. 72] Overall, it can be concluded that Papuan Malay shows consistent acoustic evidence for the word stress claim by Kluge (2017) to the extent that it is non-phonemic and regularly located on the penultimate syllable. Acoustic evidence for word stress is found in all aspects of the speech signal; mainly F0 movement timing, duration per phoneme, formant displacement and spectral tilt. [p. 61] The most common stress position was the penultimate syllable, and when the ultimate syllable was stressed, the unstressed (penultimate) syllable always contained /e/. In a number of cases, however, /e/ can occur in stressed penultimate position.

Acoustic evidence for word stress is found in all aspects of the speech signal; mainly F0 movement timing, duration per phoneme, formant displacement and…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate: penultimate stress) and the existing Kaland, Himmelmann & Kluge 2019 statement (penult default, /ε/-conditioned shift to the ultima). Adds first-hand acoustic confirmation from 19 speakers' spontaneous speech (duration, formant displacement, spectral tilt, F0 timing), the explicit statement that stress is non-phonemic, the 95/5 token distribution, and the asymmetry that ultimate stress is acoustically more marked than default penultimate stress. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-phonemic and falls regularly on the penultimate syllable (90% of Kluge's 1,116 roots; 95% of the 3,437 disyllabic-word syllables analysed here); the minority ultimate-stress words have /e/ in the penult (in this corpus always), though /e/ can also bear penultimate stress, so /e/ is not the sole conditioning factor. Acoustic analysis of spontaneous narratives from 19 speakers confirms the stressed/unstressed distinction in duration per phoneme, formant displacement, spectral tilt and F0 movement timing; ultimate (non-default) stress is acoustically more strongly marked than default penultimate stress, and F0 mainly marks deviation from the penultimate default. No minimal stress pairs are reported.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (the word 'secondary' does not occur; only disyllabic words were analysed).
new_statements.exceptions: Ultimate stress in ~10% of roots (Kluge 2017) / 5% of the analysed tokens, associated with /e/ in the penultimate syllable (always so in this dataset), but 7% of penult-stressed words also contain /e/ (citing Kluge 2017 p. 96), so /e/ does not categorically reject stress; near-minimal pairs like [ˈbe.bas] 'be free' vs [be.ˈban] 'burden'; stressed /e/ is centralised rather than peripheral (sect. 4.5.2), raising the possibility of a vowel-inventory reanalysis; author cautions that stress labels were taken over from Kluge 2017, that phrase-level effects cannot be fully excluded, and that perceptual relevance is untested (later addressed by Riesberg et al. 2018/2020 and Kaland 2021).
new_statements.identity_note: Acoustic data: 19 native speakers of Papuan Malay (students at the University of Papua, aged 20-28) recorded at CELD in Manokwari, West Papua (Pear Film retellings); stress labels taken from Kluge 2017, whose fieldwork was predominantly in the Sarmi region (north coast, Papua province). The paper treats these as one variety, Papuan Malay, distinct from Ambonese, Kupang, Larantuka and Manado Malay, which it reviews separately.

tone_statements.citation: Kaland, Constantijn. 2026. Prominence and Grouping in Papuan Malay Prosody Perception. Language and Speech (online first, 00(0)): 1-32. doi:10.1177/00238309261455331
tone_statements.quote: Unlike previous studies focusing on just a few acoustic cues, the current experiments test the effects of duration, intensity, spectral tilt and vowel quality, which all play a role in signaling word stress in Papuan Malay (Kaland, 2019). Note that F0 was found to weakly correlate with word stress and rather signaled phrase intonation (e.g., Kaland, 2019; Kaland & Baumann, 2020), in line with typological accounts on the limited role of F0 in word stress (Gordon, 2014; Gordon & Roettger, 2017). Given the focus of this study on word-level prosody, F0 is therefore not taken into account.
tone_statements.locator: p. 7, sect. 1.5 'Research Aims'; see also p. 3, sect. 1.1 (largest F0 movements phrase-final = phrase accent + boundary tone)
tone_statements.summary: F0 is not a word-level cue: it correlates only weakly with word stress and signals phrase intonation (largest F0 movements phrase-final, a phrase accent plus boundary tone). No lexical tone discussed.

sources.quote: p. 1: "Even though word stress does not appear to be lexically stored (Kaland, 2024), several experimental results indicate that this language still has a form of regular word prominence that could be termed 'word stress' (e.g., Kaland, 2019, 2021; Kaland et al., 2021; Kluge, 2017)." p. 2: "The core aim in a series of quantitative studies was to verify the claim that there is regular penultimate word stress, unless schwa is in the penultimate syllable (then stress is ultimate), as put forward for Papuan Malay (Kluge, 2017) [...] acoustic analyses of spontaneously produced speech showed that duration, spectral tilt and vowel quality were the strongest correlates of word stress (Kaland, 2019)." p. 8: "They were all Papuan Malay roots (no loanwords) with a CV.CV syllable structure and word stress on the first (penultimate) syllable, that is, the default stress pattern in this language." p. 25: "Papuan Malay listeners indeed use all acoustic cues to allocate prominences. Duration and spectral tilt appeared to be stronger cues than intensity and vowel quality, as the latter two cues only had an effect as enhanced contrast (Table 11, tapping)."

sources.citation: Kaland, Constantijn. 2024. When recall gets stressful: comparing Papuan Malay and German listeners' lexical storage of word stress. Laboratory Phonology 15(1): 1-27. doi:10.16995/labphon.11695
sources.quote: Recent studies indicated that Papuan Malay, spoken in the Eastern provinces of Indonesia, has regular penultimate word stress. Only when schwa occurs in the penultimate syllable, stress is ultimate, making the pattern highly predictable. [...] Results show that Papuan Malay listeners have worse stress recall performance than German listeners, suggesting that Papuan Malay stress is not stored lexically. (p. 1) -- The current results rather indicate that Papuan Malay listeners do not have experience in memorizing stress patterns. Note, however, that this does not necessarily mean that their language does not have regular word stress. [...] The type of stress in Papuan Malay is therefore likely to be “assigned” at a later stage in word production, i.e., after lexical retrieval. (p. 22)

sources.quote: p. 3: 'This is also the analysis proposed for PM by Kluge (2017). ... Kluge concludes that 964 (90%) of all words have penultimate stress ... and only 108 (10%) have stress on the final syllable. Of the 108 words that displayed ultimate stress, 105 (97%) contained the front open-mid vowel /ɛ/ ... in the penultimate syllable. Yet, Kluge notes that /ɛ/ does not condition ultimate stress ... Importantly, Kluge's analysis is exclusively based on her own auditory judgment'. p. 1: perception experiments 'support the claim made in earlier (production) studies that Malayic varieties appear to lack stress (i.e., lexical stress as well as post-lexical pitch accents).'
sources.locator: abstract p. 1; sect. 2.1, p. 3; sect. 6 'Conclusion', p. 32
sources.note: Extended RPT study (PM and German listeners). Restates Kluge's penultimate-default distribution and the /ɛ/ exceptions as the standing description, notes it rests on auditory judgment with 'some, though not particularly strong' acoustic support from Kaland 2019, and concludes (p. 32) that PM listeners 'show very little agreement on prosodic prominences when judging excerpts from their native language' — i.e. PM may lack lexical stress as a perceived category. Refines; a caution line for the record, no change to position.

sources.note: Rapid Prosody Transcription perception study. Accepts Kluge's 90% penultimate / 10% final distribution as the description of where the regular prominence sits, but argues that native listeners do not perceive it as a prominence distinction, so 'lexical stress' in the standard sense may not exist in Malayic varieties. Refines (a caution on the status of stress), does not contradict the penultimate coding.

tone.quote: For Papuan Malay, f0 was found to be a weak correlate of word stress, whereas duration, vowel quality and spectral tilt were more strongly correlated with word stress (Kaland 2019). Contrastive focus did not show any eﬀects on f0 contours (Kaland et al. 2023; Kaland and Himmelmann 2020). At the phrase-level, the largest f0 movements were found in ﬁnal positions, which was interpreted as having a boundary marking function … This seems to conﬁrm that f0 is at most a weak correlate of word stress in Papuan Malay (Kaland 2019).
tone.locator: aop p. 6, sect. 1.2 "F0 in Malay prosody" + aop p. 21, sect. 4 Discussion

sources.citation: Kaland, Constantijn & Nikolaus P. Himmelmann. 2020. Time-series analysis of F0 in Papuan Malay contrastive focus. Proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Speech Prosody 2020 (Tokyo), 230-234. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2020-47
sources.note: First-hand production experiment (GAMM analysis of F0 contours): F0 is not used to mark contrastive focus; the only systematic F0 events are phrase-final boundary movements on the last syllable (rise = continuation, fall = finality) plus a rise on the pre-final syllable; F0 direction correlates only weakly with word stress, i.e. pitch functions at the phrase level, not the word level. No lexical tone or pitch accent contrast is posited (none is discussed as existing); the paper does not contain the literal sentence 'Papuan Malay has no lexical tone'.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Speech Prosody 2020 (Tokyo)

tone.quote: Results show that speakers of Papuan Malay do not use F0 to mark contrastive focus and support the idea that prosodic phenomena are confined to the final syllable(s) in a phrase. [...] Concerning the boundary phenomena, systematic marking of continuation (antecedent phrase) and finality (target phrase) on the final syllable in the phrase was found. The former was indicated by a rising F0, whereas the latter was indicated by a falling F0. [...] Furthermore, the direction of F0 movements was found to correlate only weakly with word stress in Papuan Malay in [14], in line with the crosslinguistic observation that F0 is a better correlate of phrase prosody than it is of word prosody [26].

sources.quote: The current study investigates the extent to which Papuan Malay phrase prosody is used for demarcating and highlighting, taking into account the potential influence of word stress. This is done by means of acoustic analyses on a corpus of spontaneous speech. Both the form (F0 movement) and the possible functions (demarcating and highlighting) of the final two syllables in Papuan Malay phrases are investigated. Although most results favor the demarcating function of Papuan Malay phrase prosody, a highlighting function cannot be ruled out.
sources.note: Phrase-level F0 study; the abstract says nothing about where word stress falls. Its ICPhS 2019 precursor (Kaland & Baumann 2019, downloaded, see extra item) treats stress position as given ('the frequent occurrence of penultimate stress') and finds F0 movements do not correlate with word stress.

sources.quote: The current study investigates to what extent repetition reduction occurs in Papuan Malay ... An acoustic analysis is carried out on repeated words in short stories produced by native Papuan Malay speakers. The results show that upon repetition, words were shortened and produced with higher F0. In a subsequent word identification task, it was found that first and second mentions were equally intelligible.
sources.note: Discourse-level reduction of repeated words (duration, F0); nothing on word-stress position. Its Speech Prosody 2018 precursor (held by the project) is likewise silent on stress placement.
